title: Ohm’s law; ohmic and non-ohmic conductors

p: **Resistance** is a material’s opposition to the flow of electric charge. **R = V/I**, in ohm (Ω): 1 Ω = 1 V·A⁻¹.
**Ohm’s law:** the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across the conductor at constant temperature.
Learn it in this order: **the current** … depends on **the pd** … **at constant temperature**.

screens.q: Which sentence is Ohm’s law, as SAGS gives it?
choices: The potential difference is directly proportional to the current.
The wrong way round. The current depends on the pd, not the other way round. (IEB Examiners’ Report 2020)
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across the conductor at constant temperature.
The SAGS sentence: current first, and “at constant temperature”.
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
“At constant temperature” is missing, and it carries a mark.

p: Change the pd with a rheostat, read I and V, and plot a graph. A straight line through the origin means **direct proportion**.
The pd is the cause, so this book plots **I (y-axis) against V (x-axis)**. Exam graphs may swap the axes: **read the axis titles first**.

rules: The **ammeter** is in series with X.
Small currents, and switching off between readings, keep the **temperature constant**.

p: An **ohmic** conductor gives a straight line through the origin: R stays the same.
A filament bulb is **non-ohmic**: more current, a hotter filament, more resistance.
On I–V axes the gradient is **1/R**. On V–I axes it is **R**.

rules: A **straight line through the origin** means ohmic.
On I–V axes the gradient is **1/R**; on V–I axes it is **R**.
The bulb’s V/I **grows as it heats**.
On a curve, **R = V/I at the point**, not the gradient.

screens.q: A resistor carries 0,40 A when the pd across it is 6,0 V. Calculate its resistance.

traps: R = V/I: divide V by I, not multiply.

screens.q: An I–V graph (I on the y-axis, V on the x-axis) is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 0,25 A·V⁻¹. What is the resistance?
choices: On I–V axes the gradient is 1/R, not R.
4 Ω
R = 1/gradient = 1/0,25 = 4 Ω.
You cannot tell from a gradient.
For a straight line through the origin you can: on I–V axes the gradient is 1/R.
screens.why: On I against V axes the gradient is 1/R, so R = 1/0,25 = 4,00 Ω. A steeper I–V line means a smaller resistance.

screens.q: On a curve, R = V/I **at the point**, not the gradient. A filament bulb carries 0,36 A at 3 V. Calculate its resistance at that point.

traps: R = V/I: divide, do not multiply.

screens.why: R = V/I = 3/0,36 = 8,33 Ω. At 6 V the same bulb has 6/0,51 = 11,76 Ω: its resistance rises as it heats.
